{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "The kettle had gone cold by the time either of them spoke again. He had filled it out of habit, the way he filled it every afternoon at four whether anyone wanted tea or not, and now it sat on the ring with the gas off beneath it, a small failure neither would mention.

"She'll want an answer," he said.

"She'll want a great many things."

He set the broom against the wall. It slid a little and he caught it and set it again, more carefully, and the second time it stayed. She watched him do this and did not help, and it was not unkindness. There were things in the shop he was allowed to do badly, and the broom was one of them.

The card had a robin on the front. She had seen that much when he turned it over, and it was enough. Her mother had sent robins for twenty years, robins at Christmas and robins in June and a robin the week her father was buried, as though the bird carried the whole of what she meant and the words inside were only there for the post office.

"Halloran said the Dempseys are selling," he said.

"They've been selling since Easter."

"He said it as if it was news."

"Everything's news to Halloran."

She lifted her hand at last and there was nothing under it but the card, exactly as it had been, and the counter beneath the card, worn pale where the coins went down. She picked it up. She did not open it. She put it in the pocket of her apron, against her hip, where it made no shape at all.

"I'll do the kettle," she said, and did."}
